newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Labour costs seen hampering Asian coffee output.
newsitem.headline: Labour costs seen hampering Asian coffee output.

text.p: Asia's burgeoning coffee production could be hampered by oversupply and rising labour costs fuelled by strong economic growth, a U.N. body said in a report on Thursday.

"Asian coffee producers are well on track to double their share of global production from the 1980s to 2000, spearheaded by the significant increase in output in Vietnam," said the Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP).

"Indeed, it was forecast that Asia's share of production should hit 25 percent (of global output) by the year 2000, up from 10 percent in the 1980s," the report said. "This trend was further estimated to be maintained."
But there were problems, it added.
"These are an oversupply of Asian robusta coffee and higher labour costs caused by Southeast (Asia's) strong economic growth," the report said.
The report was presented at a one-day closed-door meeting of the Asia-Pacific Consultative Forum on Coffee which groups regional producers such as Indonesia, India and Thailand.
The gathering follows a three-day meeting on the tropical resort island of Bali of the 61-member International Coffee Organisation (ICO) which links producers and consuming countries.
Asian countries primarily produce robusta, which is known for its bitter flavour and is mixed with the higher priced arabica in proportions considered a trade secret.

Indonesia is the world's top robusta producer and is third in overall coffee production after Brazil and Colombia. Vietnam is also a major robusta producer, and other regional producers include India, Thailand, Papua New Guinea and Sri Lanka.
The ESCAP report said Asia-Pacific coffee production rose 3.9 percent to 1.06 million tonnes in 1995 from the previous year, benefiting from low production costs and young trees.
"The major significant coffee production increase from the region comes from Vietnam, which registered 185,000 tonnes in 1995 against 166,000 tonnes in the previous year," it said.

"Vietnam is said to be especially favourable for high productivity and low costs, which might assist Vietnam to raise coffee production to 300,000 tonnes while Indonesia coffee outputs decrease slowly," the report said without giving details.

The report said exports from the Asia-Pacific region rose 11.6 percent to 883,300 tonnes in 1994 from the previous year. It said that in 1994, Indonesia's exports decreased to 289,300 tonnes in 1994 from 349,900 tonnes in 1993.
It said Vietnam's exports rose to 156,200 tonnes in 1994 from 106,400 tonnes the previous year.
The report said India's coffee industry remained adversely affected by the lack of adequate infrastructure such as roads, communications, transportation, storage and power.
It said projections for 2000 showed that India would step up its efforts to raise production and export more as well as raise domestic consumption.

The report said a labour shortage and higher wages during the harvest season were among problems affecting development of the Thai coffee industry, while insufficient information on production and trade were also seen as obstacles.
